name: Grove Buzzer (v1.1b)
description: Active 12 mm buzzer (built-in oscillator, resonant 2300 ± 300 Hz, at least 85 dB) on a Grove board with its own transistor driver: SIG goes through a 1 kΩ resistor to an S9013 NPN transistor, which switches the buzzer's - lead to GND while its + lead sits on VCC. SIG high = beep, low = silent; no tone generation needed. Works from 3.3 V or 5 V, and a 3.3 V GPIO only supplies the ~2.6 mA base current. Sold as: Seeed Studio Grove - Buzzer v1.1b (SKU 107020000), 4-pin Grove connector SIG, NC, VCC, GND.
eli5: A little beeper with its own tone inside: set the pin high and it beeps, set it low and it goes quiet.

pins.name: SIG
pins.description: Control input (Grove pin 1, yellow wire): high = beep, low = silent. Drives the S9013 base through 1 kΩ, about 2.6 mA from a 3.3 V GPIO. There is no pull-down on the board, so drive it low at start-up rather than leaving it floating.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Buzzer supply (Grove pin 3, red wire): 3.3 V or 5 V. The buzzer current flows from this pin through the buzzer and the transistor to GND, not through SIG. Louder on 5 V.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (Grove pin 4, black wire), shared with the microcontroller.

buildNotes: Grove connector order (Seeed v1.1b Eagle schematic, J1, and the board silkscreen): pin 1 SIG (yellow), pin 2 NC (white), pin 3 VCC (red), pin 4 GND (black). The board has a 2 mm Grove socket, not header pins: use a Grove-to-female-jumper cable to reach the breadboard.

Circuit (Seeed v1.1b schematic): SIG → R1 1 kΩ → S9013 NPN base; emitter to GND; collector to the buzzer's - lead; buzzer + to VCC. SIG high = beep. There is no base pull-down resistor, so set the pin as an output driven low before anything else.

It is an active buzzer: it makes its own ~2.3 kHz tone from plain DC (Seeed spec: resonant frequency 2300 ± 300 Hz, at least 85 dB). Just switch SIG high and low. PWM on SIG only chops that tone on and off, so it cannot play clean melodies; use a passive buzzer for those.
VCC 3.3 V or 5 V both work (Seeed spec); it is louder on 5 V. The buzzer current (a few tens of mA) comes from VCC through the S9013 (500 mA max), never from the GPIO.
Version 1.0 boards (2010) had no transistor and drove the buzzer straight from SIG; this part models v1.1 and later (S9013 added May 2014).

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

buzzer = Pin({SIG}, Pin.OUT, value=0)  # SIG high = beep
while True:
    buzzer.value(1)
    print('BEEP ON')
    time.sleep(1)
    buzzer.value(0)
    print('BEEP OFF')
    time.sleep(2)

test.title: The buzzer switches on, then off again
